Bioenergetics
of Exercise
& Training

Introduction

Conditioning & Energy

What is conditioning?
Training that improves your ability to meet the energy demands of a particular activity
Do different sports require different conditioning?
Yes — sports differ in duration and intensity, so their energy demands differ
How is this energy supplied?
At the molecular level, energy is supplied in the form of ATP
Where does this ATP come from?
From the three energy systems — phosphagen, glycolytic and oxidative — depending on the intensity and duration of the activity

Section A — Terminology & ATP
Terminology & ATP
Bioenergetics
  • Flow of energy in a biological system
  • Conversion of macronutrients (carbohydrate, protein, fats) into usable energy to perform biological work
Metabolism
  • Metabolism = anabolism + catabolism
Catabolism = exergonic
  • Breakdown of large molecules → smaller molecules with release of energy
Example
  • Protein → amino acids
Energy direction
  • Catabolism releases energy
Anabolism = endergonic
  • Synthesis of larger molecules from smaller ones, using energy from catabolic reactions
Example
  • Amino acids → proteins
Energy direction
  • Anabolism uses energy
Exergonic
  • Energy released
  • Example: catabolism
Endergonic
  • Energy used
  • Example: anabolism
Energy flow
  • Energy released by exergonic reactions is used in endergonic reactions
High-energy bonds
  • Orange bonds = high-energy bonds
  • Breaking the γP–βP bond releases energy
What it powers
  • Muscle contraction
  • Ca²⁺ pumping
  • Na⁺-K⁺ gradient maintenance
Limited stores
  • Muscle cells store very little ATP — 80–100 g (≈3 oz) total
  • Must be constantly resynthesised during exercise
Energy currency
  • ATP is the universal energy currency — directly powers all endergonic biological work
  • Food energy must first be converted to ATP
ADP and Pᵢ
  • ADP = adenosine diphosphate (two phosphate groups)
  • Pᵢ = inorganic phosphate
AMP
  • Further hydrolysis of ADP removes a second phosphate → AMP (adenosine monophosphate)
Energy source
  • Energy is released primarily from ATP hydrolysis, secondarily from ADP
ATP hydrolysis
  • ATP + H₂O ⇌ ADP + Pᵢ + H⁺ + Energy
  • Catalysed by ATPase
Water and protons
  • Hydrolysis requires one H₂O
  • The H⁺ produced contributes to metabolic acidosis at high intensities
Myosin ATPase
  • Catalyzes hydrolysis for crossbridge recycling during contraction
Calcium ATPase
  • Pumps Ca²⁺ back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum after contraction
Na⁺-K⁺ ATPase
  • Maintains the sarcolemmal gradient after depolarization
Note
  • Each ATPase serves a specific site — all requiring continuous ATP
Steady state
  • ATP supply equals demand → exercise continues without fatigue
Example
  • Comfortable aerobic run
Fatigue
  • ATP supply does not meet demand — the system fails to sustain output
Example
  • Max sprint late in game
ATP at maximal fatigue
  • ATP may decrease by up to 50–60% of pre-exercise levels — never fully depleted
Training effect
  • Conditioning improves the system’s capacity to supply ATP — fatigue delayed
Key point
  • Training doesn’t change ATP demand; it improves the body’s capacity to supply it

Section B — Energy Systems
The Three Energy Systems
Three systems replenish ATP
  • Phosphagen (anaerobic)
  • Glycolytic (anaerobic)
  • Oxidative (aerobic)
Rate vs capacity
  • Phosphagen: highest rate, very short duration
  • Oxidative: slowest rate, greatest capacity
What it is
  • Stored ATP and creatine phosphate (CP)
  • Active at the start of all exercise regardless of intensity
Where
  • Sarcoplasm — anaerobic
What it is
  • Breaks down glucose or glycogen via multiple enzymatic steps
Where
  • Sarcoplasm — anaerobic
What it is
  • Carbohydrate, fat, and protein substrates
Where
  • Mitochondria — aerobic
Definition
  • Does not require oxygen to produce ATP
Systems
  • Phosphagen and glycolytic systems — both occur in the sarcoplasm
Fuel
  • Only carbohydrate can be metabolized for energy without direct oxygen involvement
Dominates
  • During high-intensity, short-duration exercise (sprints, heavy resistance training)
Definition
  • Requires oxygen as the terminal electron acceptor
Systems
  • Krebs cycle and electron transport chain occur in the mitochondria
Fuel
  • Can oxidize carbohydrate, fat, and protein — all three macronutrients
Dominates
  • During low-intensity, long-duration exercise (marathon, cycling)
Section C

Phosphagen
System

Phosphagen-system reactions
ATP hydrolysis
ATP + H₂O ⇌ ADP + Pᵢ + H⁺ + Energy
Catalysed by ATPase
Creatine kinase reaction
ADP + CP ⇌ ATP + creatine
Catalysed by creatine kinase
Adenylate kinase (myokinase) reaction
2 ADP ⇌ ATP + AMP
Catalysed by adenylate kinase
⇌ Two-way arrow: reactant and product concentrations drive the direction
Image
Section C — Phosphagen System
The Phosphagen System
ATP
  • Total body ATP store: 80–100 g (≈3 oz) — must be constantly resynthesised
  • Max ATP depletion 50–60% — never fully depleted (basic cellular function requires a minimum)
Creatine phosphate
  • CP is 4–6× higher than ATP — key short-term reserve
  • CP primary use 0–6 s: dominant for extremely high-intensity efforts ≤6 s
  • Type II fibres contain more CP than type I — advantage for explosive athletes
Note
  • Dynamic actions producing external work deplete phosphagens more than isometric actions
  • CP is stored in small amounts — once depleted, glycolysis and the oxidative system take over
Creatine kinase reaction
  • ADP + CP ⇌ ATP + creatine
  • Catalysed by creatine kinase
Terms
  • CP = creatine phosphate (PCr)
  • Creatine = free creatine (rephosphorylated later)
Function
  • CP supplies a phosphate group that combines with ADP to rapidly resynthesize ATP
  • Creatine kinase maintains ATP concentration — a rapid buffer, not a large reserve
Reversible
  • The ⇌ arrow means this reaction is reversible
  • During recovery, CP is rebuilt from free creatine via aerobic metabolism
Adenylate kinase (myokinase) reaction
  • 2 ADP ⇌ ATP + AMP
  • Catalysed by adenylate kinase
  • Two ADP donate a phosphate between themselves — one becomes ATP, the other AMP
Emergency ATP source
  • Single-enzyme reaction that rapidly resynthesises ATP when ATP and CP are depleted
  • Secondary but important during maximal efforts
Glycolysis signal
  • AMP produced is a powerful glycolysis stimulant — signals critically low energy, activates PFK
  • AMP allosterically activates PFK — the rate-limiting glycolytic enzyme
  • Bridges phosphagen and glycolytic systems
Law of mass action
  • ATP hydrolysis, creatine kinase and adenylate kinase reactions follow the law of mass action (mass action effect)
  • Reactant/product concentrations drive reaction direction
Example
ATP hydrolysis → ADP + Pᵢ rise → creatine kinase and adenylate kinase accelerate
Near-equilibrium reactions
  • The phosphagen-system reactions are near-equilibrium reactions
  • Direction dictated by reactant concentrations
Slowing or reversing
  • When ATP rises (exercise stops or intensity drops), reactions slow or reverse
  • Free creatine is rephosphorylated to CP via aerobic metabolism during recovery
ATP stabilises
  • When glycolysis or oxidative system can supply ATP, creatine kinase slows — ATP stabilises
  • Continues until exercise stops or intensity drops enough to spare CP
Self-regulating
  • Rising ADP drives resynthesis; rising ATP slows/reverses
  • Concentration gradients control rate — no complex enzyme activation
ATP
  • Full resynthesis ~3–5 min post-exercise
CP
  • Full resynthesis 3–8 min; up to 8 min after maximal effort
  • Half replenished in ~30 s — enables repeated maximal efforts
Rest intervals
  • CP half-life = 30 s — basis for short rest intervals
  • Full recovery 3–8 min — critical for programming maximal-effort sets
Resistance training
  • Increases resting phosphagen concentration in the triceps brachii after 5 weeks
  • Likely via type II fibre hypertrophy
Repletion is aerobic
  • Repletion is primarily aerobic
  • Aerobic capacity matters for power athletes
Section D

Glycolytic
System

Glycolysis
Image
Section D — Glycolysis
Glycolysis
What it is
  • Breakdown of carbohydrate (muscle glycogen or blood glucose) to resynthesize ATP via multiple enzymatic steps
  • Occurs in the sarcoplasm
Rate vs phosphagen
  • Rate is slower than phosphagen, but capacity is much higher
  • Glycogen and glucose supply is far greater than CP
End product
  • End product = pyruvate
  • Fate depends on energy demand and O₂ availability
2 ATP net
  • 4 produced − 2 consumed (hexokinase + PFK)
3 ATP net
  • 4 produced − 1 consumed (bypasses hexokinase — already phosphorylated)
  • Glycogen is broken down by glycogenolysis (enzyme: glycogen phosphorylase)
Why glycogen beats glucose
  • Muscle glycogen is already phosphorylated — the hexokinase ATP cost is bypassed
  • This is why maintaining glycogen through nutrition directly supports performance
Sarcoplasm
  • Same compartment as phosphagen — no mitochondrial transport needed
Pyruvate
  • End product of glycolysis
  • Fate depends on energy demand and O₂
Fork in the road
  • Controlled by cellular energy demand
  • High demand: lactate (fast)
  • Lower demand + O₂: mitochondria (slow)
Note
  • Glycolysis itself doesn’t require oxygen — “aerobic/anaerobic” labels describe outcomes only
Pyruvate to lactate
  • Pyruvate → lactate via lactate dehydrogenase
  • Regenerates NAD⁺
Characteristics
  • Higher ATP rate, limited duration — H⁺ accumulation → metabolic acidosis
  • Also: anaerobic glycolysis
Dominates
  • At high energy demand (resistance training, sprinting)
Pyruvate to mitochondria
Pyruvate → mitochondria → acetyl-CoA → Krebs cycle
Characteristics
  • Slower rate, longer duration if intensity and O₂ allow
  • Also: aerobic glycolysis
Dominates
  • At lower intensities
Where the H⁺ comes from
ATP hydrolysis
ATP + H₂O ⇌ ADP + Pᵢ + H⁺ + Energy
Catalysed by ATPase
H⁺ is a product of ATP hydrolysis
The Cori cycle
Image
Section D — Lactate
Lactate & Acidosis
Lactate
  • Not a waste product — an energy substrate
H⁺ and fatigue
  • Metabolic acidosis may be responsible for much of the peripheral fatigue that occurs during exercise
The real source
  • Lactate is not the cause
  • ATP hydrolysis outside the mitochondria is the dominant H⁺ source
Lactate dehydrogenase
  • Actually consumes protons
  • Call it metabolic acidosis, not “lactic acidosis”
Effects during fatigue
  • ↓ intracellular pH
  • Inhibits glycolytic enzymes
  • Disrupts excitation-contraction coupling
  • Inhibits Ca²⁺ binding to troponin
Other fatigue factors
  • Elevated interstitial K⁺ and Pᵢ impair Ca²⁺ release from the SR
  • Metabolic acidosis alone doesn’t explain all peripheral fatigue
Not a waste product
  • Lactate is an energy substrate, especially in type I and cardiac muscle fibres
  • It can be oxidised where produced, transported to other fibres, or converted back to glucose in the liver
What influences it
  • Production rises with exercise intensity and depends on fibre type
  • Duration, training state and initial glycogen also influence accumulation
Blood lactate at rest
  • 0.5–2.2 mmol/L blood at rest
  • 0.5–2.2 mmol/kg wet muscle
Type II max production
  • 0.5 mmol·g⁻¹·s⁻¹ — twice type I (0.25 mmol·g⁻¹·s⁻¹)
Severe fatigue threshold
  • 20–25 mmol/L
  • >30 mmol/L reported after multiple bouts
Clearance
  • Returns to pre-exercise within ~1 hour
  • Peaks ~5 min post-exercise
  • Active recovery clears it faster than passive
Recovery marker
  • Clearance rate is an indirect recovery marker, not waste removal
Clearance
  • Both aerobic and anaerobic athletes clear lactate faster than untrained
Resistance training
  • Produces lactate adaptations similar to endurance training
Responses
  • Blood lactate is higher after high-intensity intermittent exercise (e.g. resistance training, sprints) than after lower-intensity continuous exercise
  • Trained people show lower lactate at a given absolute workload, but higher lactate at maximal exercise
Cori cycle
Lactate produced in muscle → enters blood → transported to the liver → converted back to glucose via gluconeogenesis → released back into blood → used by muscles
Role
  • The Cori cycle recycles lactate as a glucose precursor
  • Especially important during prolonged exercise and recovery
Takeaway
  • The Cori cycle converts lactate into glucose — making lactate an indirect glucose source
  • Lactate clearance = indirect recovery marker from metabolic acidosis
Glycolysis
Allosteric inhibition and activation
Image
Section D — Energy Yield & Regulation
Glycolysis: Yield & Control
Yield
  • Both routes yield only 2 ATP net from blood glucose
  • Gross yield = 4 ATP; net varies with glucose source (2 or 3 ATP)
Control
  • PFK = rate-limiting step of glycolysis
  • ATP = allosteric inhibitor; AMP = powerful activator
Net glycolysis (pyruvate to lactate)
  • Glucose + 2Pᵢ + 2ADP → 2Lactate + 2ATP + H₂O
Result
  • Fast glycolysis produces lactate + NAD⁺ regeneration
Net glycolysis (pyruvate to mitochondria)
  • Glucose + 2Pᵢ + 2ADP + 2NAD⁺ → 2Pyruvate + 2ATP + 2NADH + 2H₂O
Result
  • Slow glycolysis produces pyruvate + NADH for the ETC
Phosphorylation
  • Adding Pᵢ to another molecule (e.g. ADP + Pᵢ → ATP)
Substrate-level phosphorylation
  • ATP made directly in the metabolic pathway, without the ETC
Two ATP-generating reactions
  • Phosphoglycerate kinase: 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate → 3-phosphoglycerate + ATP
  • Pyruvate kinase: phosphoenolpyruvate → pyruvate + ATP
Yield
  • Gross yield = 4 ATP
  • Net varies depending on glucose source (2 or 3 ATP)
  • Fast, but limited yield
Regulatory enzyme #1
  • Phosphorylates glucose → glucose-6-phosphate, trapping it in the cell
Regulation
  • Allosterically inhibited by glucose-6-phosphate
  • Commits glucose to glycolysis
Rate-limiting enzyme
  • Fructose-6-phosphate → fructose-1,6-bisphosphate
  • Bottleneck and most important regulator
Inhibited by
  • ATP, CP, citrate, low pH
Activated by
  • ADP, AMP, Pᵢ, ammonia
Regulatory enzyme #3
  • Catalyses phosphoenolpyruvate → pyruvate (final step)
Inhibited by
  • ATP, acetyl-CoA
Activated by
  • AMP, fructose-1,6-bisphosphate
Stimulate
  • High ADP, Pᵢ, AMP, ammonia + slight ↓ pH
  • Signs of increased ATP hydrolysis
Inhibit
  • High ATP, CP, citrate, free fatty acids + marked ↓ pH
  • Signs of adequate energy at rest
Takeaway
  • PFK = rate-limiting step of glycolysis
  • ATP = allosteric inhibitor; AMP = powerful activator
Lactate threshold and OBLA
Image
Section D — Lactate Threshold
Lactate Threshold
Lactate threshold (LT / LT1)
  • Intensity at which blood lactate begins an abrupt rise above baseline
Second break point
  • OBLA / LT2 — a second exponential lactate rise at higher intensities
Training
  • Training at/above LT or OBLA shifts both thresholds right
What it is
  • Intensity at which blood lactate begins an abrupt rise above baseline
  • Marks significantly increased reliance on the glycolytic pathway
Ventilatory threshold
  • Corresponds with the ventilatory threshold — used as the anaerobic threshold marker
Untrained
  • 50–60% VO₂max in untrained individuals
Mechanism
  • LT corresponds to the recruitment of intermediate and large motor units (type II fibres)
  • Particularly suited for anaerobic metabolism and lactate production
Training shifts LT right
  • Aerobically trained athletes reach LT at a higher relative intensity — more work before significant lactate accumulation
Trained value
  • 70–80% VO₂max in aerobically trained athletes
Shift caused by
  • Reduced catecholamine release
  • Increased mitochondrial content
  • Greater reliance on free fatty acids to meet ATP demand
Key adaptation
  • Training at/above LT intensity pushes the threshold right — the athlete can work at higher %VO₂max before lactate accumulates
  • This is the key aerobic adaptation for performance
What it is
  • Onset of Blood Lactate Accumulation, also LT2
  • A second exponential lactate rise at higher intensities
Value
  • ~4 mmol/L blood lactate at the second inflection point
  • Calculable via the Dmax modified method
Training
  • Training at/above LT or OBLA shifts both thresholds right
  • Lactate accumulates later, at higher %VO₂max, with less metabolic acidosis

Oxidative
(Aerobic)
System

Image
Section E — Oxidative System
Oxidative Substrates
Substrate use
  • The oxidative system uses carbohydrate, fat and (minimally) protein
  • Fat dominates at rest — the oxidative system has time to run at full capacity at low demand
What drives the shift
  • As intensity rises, substrate shifts fat → carbohydrate
  • As duration increases at submaximal intensity, it shifts back → fat
  • Glycogen availability drives the transition
At rest
  • 70% fat, 30% carbohydrate
Why
  • Fat dominates because the oxidative system has time to run at full capacity at low demand
High-intensity aerobic exercise
  • Shift toward ~100% carbohydrate if adequate supply is available
  • Only minimal contributions from fats and protein
Prolonged submaximal work
  • Gradual shift back to fat as glycogen depletes
Short-term exercise
  • Minimal — negligible during most short-duration activities
Prolonged exercise (>90 min)
  • 3–18% — increases during prolonged activity and long-term starvation
Primary amino acids
  • BCAAs: leucine, isoleucine, valine
  • Major amino acids oxidised in skeletal muscle
How it enters metabolism
Proteins → amino acids → glucose (gluconeogenesis), pyruvate, or Krebs intermediates → ATP
Link
  • Links protein metabolism to glucose availability during prolonged exercise
Nitrogenous waste
  • Degradation → nitrogenous waste via urea and ammonia
  • Ammonia is toxic and fatigue-associated — relevant during high-volume training
Glycolysis
The Krebs cycle

Electron transport chain
Image
Section E — Glucose Oxidation
Glucose Oxidation
The pathway
Glycolysis (sarcoplasm) → Pyruvate oxidation (mitochondrial matrix) → Krebs cycle (mitochondrial matrix) → ETC (inner mitochondrial membrane)
Pyruvate dehydrogenase complex
  • Pyruvate → acetyl-CoA (2C)
  • One carbon lost as CO₂; yields 1 NADH per pyruvate
Krebs cycle
  • Also: citric acid cycle; tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle
  • Continues substrate oxidation
ATP
  • Produces 2 ATP per glucose indirectly via GTP (1 per turn)
Output per glucose (2 turns)
  • 6 NADH · 2 FADH₂ · 2 ATP (GTP) · 4 CO₂
Role
  • NADH and FADH₂ carry H to the ETC for bulk ATP production
  • Main role: generating NADH and FADH₂ to power the ETC
Decarboxylations
  • Isocitrate → α-ketoglutarate: 1 NADH + CO₂
  • α-Ketoglutarate → succinyl-CoA: 1 NADH + CO₂ (second decarboxylation)
Substrate-level phosphorylation
  • Succinyl-CoA → succinate: 1 GTP (= 1 ATP)
  • Only substrate-level phosphorylation in Krebs — direct ATP equivalent
FADH₂ and NADH
  • Succinate → fumarate: 1 FADH₂ (catalysed by succinate dehydrogenase)
  • Malate → oxaloacetate: 1 NADH — regenerates oxaloacetate, restarts the cycle
Per turn (1 acetyl-CoA)
  • 3 NADH + 1 FADH₂
  • 1 GTP + 2 CO₂
NADH + H⁺
  • 2.5 ATP per NADH
FADH₂
  • 1.5 ATP per FADH₂
Traditional values
  • Traditional biochemistry cites 3 ATP per NADH and 2 per FADH₂
Why NADH > FADH₂
  • They enter the ETC at different sites
NADH enters earlier → passes through more proton-pumping complexes → larger proton gradient → more ATP
FADH₂ enters later → fewer pumps → less ATP
Cytochromes
  • Electron carrier proteins
  • H atoms passed down the chain create a proton gradient that drives ATP synthase
Final step
  • O₂ accepts final electrons → H₂O
Definition
  • ATP production during the ETC is termed oxidative phosphorylation
>90% of ATP synthesis
  • It accounts for >90% of all ATP synthesis in aerobic conditions
  • Far exceeding substrate-level phosphorylation in glycolysis and the Krebs cycle combined
Totals
  • Substrate-level (glycolysis + Krebs) provides 4 ATP total (2 + 2)
  • Oxidative phosphorylation (ETC) provides 28 ATP (5 + 5 + 15 + 3)
  • This is why the oxidative system has the greatest ATP capacity
Role
  • The ETC is where the NADH and FADH₂ collected across all three stages are finally converted into usable ATP

Image
Section E — Fat Oxidation & Control
Fat Oxidation & Control
Fat oxidation
  • Greatest ATP production capacity of all energy systems
  • Fat has enormous ATP capacity but is rate-limited — can’t supply ATP fast enough for high-intensity work
Fat to ATP
Triglycerides → free fatty acids → beta oxidation → Krebs + ETC
Steps
  • Triglycerides: hormone-sensitive lipase → free fatty acids + glycerol
  • Free fatty acids: enter muscle fibres → transported into mitochondria
  • Beta oxidation: fatty acids → acetyl-CoA + NADH + FADH₂
  • Acetyl-CoA enters the Krebs cycle; NADH/FADH₂ go to the ETC for a large ATP yield
Palmitic acid
  • A single 16-carbon fatty acid yields >100 ATP
  • A triglyceride of three 16C fatty acids yields >300 ATP — far exceeding 32 ATP from one glucose
At rest
  • 70% of energy from fats at rest
  • Dominates at rest/low intensity — greatest ATP capacity despite slow rate
Carbohydrate
  • Carbohydrate essential during intense exercise even when fat is abundant
Isocitrate dehydrogenase
  • Slowest reaction: isocitrate → α-ketoglutarate, catalysed by isocitrate dehydrogenase
  • Stimulated by ADP, inhibited by ATP
Summary
  • Isocitrate dehydrogenase = rate-limiting
  • ADP stimulates, ATP inhibits Krebs + ETC
Carrier availability
  • Insufficient NAD⁺/FAD²⁺ → Krebs cycle slows
  • If NADH/FADH₂ carriers are saturated, the Krebs cycle slows
Coupled
  • ETC must run fast enough to regenerate carriers — ETC and Krebs are directly coupled
  • NAD⁺/FAD²⁺ availability couples ETC to Krebs rate
ETC regulation
  • ETC: inhibited by ATP, stimulated by ADP
GTP accumulation
  • GTP accumulation inhibits succinyl-CoA → succinate
  • This slows the initial Krebs reaction (oxaloacetate + acetyl-CoA → citrate)

Section F — Energy Production & Capacity
Energy Production & Capacity
Key principle
  • Contribution depends primarily on intensity, secondarily on duration — regardless of aerobic fitness
All three, always
  • At no time does any single system provide complete energy supply
  • Assumes best-effort performance
  • As duration increases, aerobic contribution grows
  • Events range from 1–3 s (snatch, shot put) to >4 h (ultramarathon)
Inverse relationship
  • Rate vs capacity
  • Phosphagen = fastest rate, least capacity
  • Fat oxidation = slowest rate, greatest capacity

Section G

Substrate
Depletion &
Repletion

Image
Section G — Substrate Depletion & Repletion
Depletion & Repletion
Selective depletion
  • Energy substrates (phosphagens, glucose, glycogen, lactate, free fatty acids, amino acids) can be selectively depleted during activities of various intensities and durations
  • The energy the bioenergetic systems can produce is then reduced
What limits performance
  • Fatigue is frequently associated with depletion of phosphagens and glycogen
  • Performance is rarely limited by depletion of free fatty acids, lactate, and amino acids
CP
  • 50–70% depleted in early high-intensity exercise (5–30 s)
  • Almost completely depleted at exhaustion
ATP
  • May decrease by up to 50–60% of pre-exercise levels during induced fatigue
  • Never fully depleted
Sustaining ATP
  • ATP is sustained via CP depletion, myokinase, and glycolysis/fat oxidation
  • Primary limit in very short maximal efforts = CP exhaustion, not ATP
CHO timing
  • 0.7–3.0 g CHO/kg every 2 h post-exercise
Peak rate
  • 5–6 mmol/g wet muscle per hour during the first 4–6 h — with optimal CHO intake
  • Full repletion within 24 h with adequate CHO intake
Eccentric exception
  • High eccentric component (muscle damage) → more time required even with adequate CHO
Training effect
  • Both anaerobic (sprint, RT) and aerobic endurance training increase resting glycogen — with adequate nutrition
At <50% VO₂max
  • Stable
  • Falls below 2.8 mmol/L only with exercise >90 min
Thresholds
  • Hypoglycaemia threshold: 2.5 mmol/L — risk increases as liver glycogen depletes
  • Critical threshold: >90 min at >50% VO₂max — when exogenous carbohydrate becomes critical
Liver vs muscle glycogen
  • Muscle glycogen is the primary fuel for moderate/high-intensity exercise
  • Liver glycogen matters more at low intensity and prolonged duration — it’s the primary regulator of blood glucose
Takeaway
  • Blood glucose is stable at <50% VO₂max but falls after 90 min at >50% VO₂max as liver glycogen depletes
  • Exogenous CHO prevents hypoglycaemia and preserves performance

Section H — Limiting Factors & O₂ Uptake
Limiting Factors & O₂ Uptake
Limiting factors
  • Which fuel or byproduct is most likely to run out first — and stop the athlete — depends entirely on the event
  • 1 = least probable limiting factor; 5 = most probable
Oxygen uptake
  • Oxygen deficit = the anaerobic cost of starting exercise
  • EPOC = VO₂ that stays elevated after exercise
What it is
  • At the start of exercise, the aerobic system responds slowly to the initial increase in energy demand
  • The anaerobic contribution during this lag period is termed the oxygen deficit
Bridging the gap
  • Anaerobic mechanisms bridge the gap until aerobic metabolism reaches steady state
Takeaway
  • The oxygen deficit is the anaerobic cost of starting exercise
  • The gap between what aerobic metabolism can supply and what the body needs in the first minutes of effort
EPOC
  • After exercise, VO₂ stays elevated above resting levels — also termed oxygen debt or recovery O₂
  • EPOC ≠ oxygen deficit — only a small to moderate relationship exists between them
Factors
  • O₂ replenishment
  • ATP/CP resynthesis
  • ↑ temperature/circulation/ventilation
  • ↑ triglyceride cycling
  • ↑ protein turnover
Greatest EPOC
  • Intensity >50–60% VO₂max + duration >40 min
Supramaximal bouts
  • Brief supramaximal bouts (>100% VO₂max) may induce the greatest EPOC with lower total work
Heavy vs circuit
  • Heavy resistance (3×8, 80–90% 1RM) produces greater EPOC than circuit training (4×15, 50% 1RM)
  • Also intensity-dependent
Takeaway
  • EPOC is intensity-dependent for both modes

Section H — Interval Training & HIIT
Interval Training & HIIT
Metabolic specificity
  • Correct intensities and rest intervals “select” specific energy systems
  • Reflects sport demands — more efficient training
HIIT
  • Targets both muscle and heart simultaneously
  • Equivalent adaptations to long slow endurance training in a fraction of the time
% Max Power Primary System Typical Time W:R Ratio
90–100% Phosphagen 5–10 s 1:12 to 1:20
75–90% Fast Glycolysis 15–30 s 1:3 to 1:5
30–75% Fast Glycolysis + Oxidative 1–3 min 1:3 to 1:4
20–30% Oxidative >3 min 1:1 to 1:3
Why long rest for phosphagen?
Full CP resynthesis = 3–8 min despite 30 s half-life — maximal efforts need the longest W:R ratios (1:12–1:20).
Metabolic specificity
Correct intensities and rest intervals "select" specific energy systems — reflects sport demands, more efficient training.
HIIT variables
  • 9 variables can be manipulated
    • Intensity of the active portion of each work bout
    • Duration of the active portion of each work bout
    • Intensity of the recovery portion of each work bout
    • Duration of the recovery portion of each work bout
    • Number of work bouts performed in each set
    • Number of sets
    • Rest time between sets
    • Recovery intensity between sets
    • Mode of exercise for HIIT
Key target metric
  • >90% VO₂max
  • Cumulative active time should reach several minutes above this
Most important variables
  • Intensity & duration
  • Of both active and recovery portions
Training adaptations
  • ↑ VO₂max
  • ↑ proton buffering
  • ↑ glycogen content
  • ↑ anaerobic thresholds
  • ↑ time to exhaustion
  • ↑ time-trial performance
Mechanism
  • Concurrent recruitment of large motor units + near-maximal cardiac output
  • Stimulus for oxidative fibre adaptation and myocardial hypertrophy
Takeaway
  • HIIT targets both muscle and heart simultaneously
  • Duty-cycle structure equivalent to any interval work-bout/rest-period
Protocols
  • HIIT: 250% VO₂peak — 4–6 × 30 s sprints
  • LSD: 90–120 min cycling at 65% VO₂peak
  • Both over 6 sessions
Results
  • Equivalent improvements in muscle buffering capacity and glycogen content
  • Comparable time-trial improvement
Takeaway
  • Same results. Far less time
  • HIIT provides equivalent physiological adaptations to long slow endurance training in a fraction of the time — the more time-efficient choice for athletes with mixed training demands

Section H — Training Types
Combining Training Modalities
Three related but distinct concepts
  • Combination, cross-training and concurrent training
  • They differ in structure, metabolic intent, and interference risk
Combination training
  • Mix of different exercise types for overall fitness — no specific structure implied
Example
  • 800m runner adding long slow runs alongside event-specific work
Cross-training
  • Different modalities sharing the same metabolic adaptation goal without overstressing primary muscles
Example
  • Runner adding rowing to build aerobic capacity
Concurrent training
  • Simultaneous anaerobic resistance + aerobic endurance — same session or day
Risk
  • Risk of interference effect on high-strength, high-power capabilities
Memory aid
  • Combination = general fitness mix
  • Cross-training = same goal, different mode
  • Concurrent = same time, highest interference risk
May reduce anaerobic capabilities via
  • ↓ rapid voluntary activation
  • Chronically low glycogen limiting intracellular signalling
  • Fibre type transition toward slow-twitch
When aerobic training helps
  • Aerobic metabolism supports post-exercise VO₂, lactate removal, and PCr restoration
Anaerobic training
  • Anaerobic training itself can improve aerobic power and recovery markers
Guidance
  • Extensive endurance training may be counterproductive for strength/power athletes
  • Use metabolically specific interval training instead of long slow distance
Takeaway
  • The interference effect is real but not absolute
  • Targeted interval training can cover aerobic needs without compromising strength and power adaptations
